newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central Africa's flamboyant emperor Bokassa dies.
newsitem.headline: Central Africa's flamboyant emperor Bokassa dies.

text.p: Jean-Bedel Bokassa, former self-proclaimed emperor of the impoverished but diamond-rich Central African Republic, combined a taste for extravagant gestures with eccentric utterances.
Bokassa, who died on Sunday aged 75, held sway over the former French colony for almost a decade and a half, during which he became notorious for the excesses and brutality of his rule.

Ousted in a 1979 French-backed coup, he was sentenced to death for murder and embezzlement after a trial coloured by accusations of cannibalism and infanticide but won his freedown after spending just seven years in jail.
He remained convinced of his popularity with the masses until the end, harbouring hopes of being allowed to stage a comeback via presidential elections scheduled for 1999.
"Whenever I go out, a large gathering collects about me out of adoration, so I seldom go out," he told Reuters in an interview at his home in the capital Bangui in May.
Around that time he wrote to President Ange-Felix Patasse asking for an amnesty so that he could run for president.

"His majesty Bokassa the First hopes that his request will be favourably received to enable him to stand as a candidate in the next presidential elections according to the principle of democracy, in line with the wishes of the majority of the Central African people," he said in the letter.
Bokassa, a fervent Roman Catholic who fathered at least 55 children, once flirted with the idea of becoming a priest.

Instead he became a soldier in France's colonial army, finishing World War Two a sergeant-major after landing with General Charles de Gaulle's Free French forces in France. France made him a member of the Legion of Honour and awarded him the Croix de Guerre.
Bokassa, armed forces chief of staff at the time, seized power in 1966, toppling his nephew David Dacko, the country's independence president.
His rule, virtually absolute, was punctuated by capricious decisions. On Mother's Day 1971 he freed all women prisoners and ordered the execution of all men convicted of assaults on women.
In the same year he ordered that thieves should have one ear cut off for one theft, two ears for two thefts, their right hands for three thefts and be executed for four.

In 1977, modelling himself on his hero Napoleon Bonaparte, he treated himself to an elaborate coronation -- his crown alone was worth $5 million and the ceremony reputedly swallowed a quarter of the country's annual foreign exchange earnings.
Bokassa was deposed in a 1979 while in Libya.

French paratroops reinstalled Dacko as president after an African jurists' commission said Bokassa had ordered, and perhaps taken part in, the massacre of around 200 schoolchildren who had complained about their uniforms.
Bokassa flew to France where he spent three days in the plane before Ivory Coast's late president Felix Houphouet-Boigny was persuaded to give him refuge.
In 1983, Bokassa tried to organise a comeback, but France tipped off Ivory Coast and police arrested him.

He was deported to France with 15 of his younger children. He lived in an 18th-century chateau outside Paris but was not a happy exile, grudgingly tolerated by the government which closely controlled his movements.

In 1986, he gave the French the slip and astonished the Republic's three million people by returning unexpectedly. After a six-month trial in 1987, he was sentenced to death for murder and embezzlement.
The then military ruler Andre Kolingba commuted the death sentence to a jail term.

Freed from prison at the height of democratic change in 1993 after serving nearly seven years of the 20-year term, Bokassa compared himself to Jesus Christ in a speech to thousands of people at the cathedral in the capital Bangui.
"I have returned after being condemned in your name like Jesus Christ was for all our sins," he said, clad in his ornate bemedalled marshal's uniform and carrying an ivory cane.
The authorities, irritated at his repeated claims to the throne, kicked him out of his presidential guest house.

He then lived quietly in Bangui on a French army pension but during an army pay revolt in May he joined critics of former colonial power France, which stepped in under a defence pact to keep Patasse in power.
"Why does France intervene in our country at every little problem, why ? Perhaps because of the diamonds," he said.
